items.title: Home
items.text:
Lilac Camera

Sony's camera app for the Xperia XZ1 Compact, rebuilt for custom ROMs, with GCam multi-frame processing

Get started For ROM maintainers

Lilac is a camera app for one phone. It rebuilds Sony's camera app, with all of the camera's hardware features, for custom ROMs, and adds GCam's multi-frame processing on top.

Fully works on sunplex07's LineageOS 23.2 only

Other lilac ROMs get basic multi-frame stacking in Photo, Night, Portrait and Video, because they lack the raw19 camera shim and Sony's cacao service. What each feature needs

1Sony's camera featuresFaces, tracking, laser focus, the camera key, stabilisers and 960 fps slow motion 2GCam's processingHDR+ and merged frames, on Sony's camera hardware 3What works on your ROMFull on sunplex07's LineageOS, basic elsewhere

items.title: Sony's camera features
items.text:
Sony's camera app uses the phone's hardware fully but does not run on custom ROMs. Lilac brings its features back: face frames, subject tracking, the laser distance sensor, the two-stage camera key, smile shutter, Sony's own photo processing, Sony's video stabilisers, and 960 fps slow motion with 60 and 120 fps video. The aim is the whole of Sony's camera app; the Sony camera features page lists what is done and what is not yet.

No code from Sony's camera app is in Lilac. Its Sony features were rebuilt by studying how Sony's app talks to the phone's camera system, which settings it sends and which system services it calls, and making the same requests from Lilac's own code. Where a feature needs Sony's own services, such as cacao for slow motion, Lilac calls the ones already on the phone's ROM; it does not ship them.

The XZ1 Compact's sensor records at 960 frames a second, but on custom ROMs that went away with Sony's camera app. sunplex07's LineageOS 23.2 keeps Sony's slow-motion service, cacao, and Lilac reaches it through its companion app, the Lilac Sony Bridge. So 960 fps works again.

Next: Sony's camera features, done and not yet

items.title: GCam's multi-frame processing
items.text:
GCam processes photos well but knows nothing about Sony's camera. Lilac runs GCam's HDR+ processing on Sony's camera hardware, next to the Sony features above.

Compared with a default camera app:

Default camera appsuch as ApertureLilac Each photoOne finished JPEG from Sony's processor3 to 20 frames merged into one: less noise, more detail Starting pointSony's picture, noise already smoothed away with detailRAW frames merged before any processing GCam Bright skiesOne exposure: what clips stays whiteA darker RAW burst; HDRNet lifts the shadows GCam Dim lightOne frame, heavily smoothedNight: 6 to 12 frames merged and brightened FocusTap a pointSubject tracking, face choice, laser distance Sony Slow motionNone960 fps at 720p Sony

GCam the same HDR+ pipeline and models as Google's camera app   Sony Sony's own camera features

What comes from GCam

PhotonCamera rebuilt GCam's HDR+ pipeline from the GCam ports MGC and AGC, to run through Android's standard camera interface on the graphics chip. Lilac's Pro mode carries it with GCam's own model files:

GCam In Lilac HDR+: a burst of darker RAW frames Pro's HDR+ frames and the darker burst Sabre, the handheld merge the Sabre merge mode (default) HDR+ spatial merge with brackets the Spatial merge mode Learned auto exposure the same models, capped by the HDR ratio (8× by default; GCam's default is 9.8×) HDRNet tone mapping the same HDRNet model Denoise tuning GCam's luma, chroma and Sabre settings

What Lilac adds: Pro photos are developed one at a time in a separate process that waits for free memory, so they fit in 4 GB; Photo, Night and Portrait stack without RAW, on every ROM; and Sony's camera features that GCam does not know.

Next: how a picture is made, from sensor to stacked photo

items.title: Rebuilt for a 4.6-inch screen
items.text:
Lilac's interface is not PhotonCamera's. The camera, the gallery and the editor were rebuilt around one rule: a 4.6-inch phone held in one hand.

Lilac in one hand The Xperia XZ1 Compact with Lilac's camera screen. An animation shows how far a right thumb reaches from the lower edge, and a touch point moving between the buttons, all inside that reach. Numbered as in the list: 1 thumb reach, 2 picture gestures, 3 shutter with the zoom control, 4 camera key and volume keys on the right side. 3s 12 M 1 2 3 4 Held in the right hand, to scale. The glow is how far the thumb reaches.
  1. Everything you press is in thumb reach. Holding the phone in one hand, your thumb reaches the lower part of the screen, shaded in the animation. Every button sits there; the top of the screen is only picture.
  2. The picture takes the gestures: swipe down for everyday settings, up for manual controls, sideways for looks.
  3. The shutter is the mode dial, with the zoom control just above it, in reach of the thumb.
  4. The side keys are camera controls: half-press the camera key to focus, press fully to shoot; the volume keys shoot or zoom.

items.title: Install the Sony bridge
items.text:
Some of Lilac's features need a small companion app, the Lilac Sony Bridge, installed as a privileged system app. If your ROM ships it, you are done: this page is not for you. This page is for testers whose ROM has Sony's slow-motion service but not the bridge.

Before you start

  • You need a computer with adb, and on the phone USB debugging and Rooted debugging (Settings › System › Developer options). Rooted debugging exists only on debug-capable (userdebug) builds such as sunplex07's LineageOS 23.2.
  • The install writes to the system partition and reboots the phone.
  • It has only been tested on sunplex07's unofficial LineageOS 23.2 for lilac.
  • Not for everyday users: if you just want slow motion, ask your ROM maintainer to include the bridge.

items.title: What it does, and what it leaves alone
items.text:
• Unlocks 960 fps slow motion at 720p in Lilac's Video mode.
  • Adds 1080p at 60 fps and 720p at 120 fps to Video.
  • Adds Sony's video stabilisation, Steady and Active.
  • Offers Lilac to other apps: see below.
  • Adds one folder, /system/priv-app/LilacSonyBridge, with one APK in it.
  • Does not touch vendor files, SELinux settings or the bootloader. bridge.sh uninstall removes everything it added.

Why a separate app: Sony's slow-motion service (cacao) only talks to privileged system apps, and its libraries can only be loaded by one. Lilac itself stays an ordinary app you can update; the bridge does the privileged part.

items.title: What the bridge adds
items.text: These features exist only in Lilac, and only with the bridge. Without it, Video simply does not offer them.

items.title: Photo and video requests from other apps
items.text:
When an app asks for a photo or a video (a messenger's camera button, a contact photo, a file upload), Android lists only cameras that came with the system. The bridge is one, so it adds a Lilac Camera entry to that list and hands the request to Lilac. The picture goes back to the app that asked.

  • The entry shows only while a Lilac signed with this project's key is installed, and only while that Lilac is not itself a system app. A system Lilac is listed on its own.
  • After installing Lilac, open it once. That is when the bridge notices it.
  • If the entry is missing, run bash bridge.sh check: the forwarder line says on or off.

items.title: More frame rates
items.text:
Video can record at:

  • 1080p at 60 fps
  • 720p at 120 fps

Both are for the rear camera at 16:9 and need good light. They show in the frame-rate step only when the bridge is installed. Details: video.

120 fps files play at full speed in other apps. Lilac's gallery plays them four times slower, and asks Slowed or Full speed when you share or export one.

items.title: Sony stabilisation
items.text: The Stabilise item in Video steps through Off, EIS+, Steady and Active, and offers each only where it works. Steady and Active are Sony's own SteadyShot and Intelligent Active. Which size and rate allow which: video.

items.title: Lilac and the bridge
items.text:
• Any newer Lilac works with your bridge: the interface between them only grows, and Lilac uses only what the installed bridge offers. A feature that needs a newer bridge says so in the release notes.
  • Signature: the bridge serves only a Lilac signed with the certificate of this project's releases (Lilac and, Lilac Beta), whatever key the bridge itself is signed with. A Lilac built and signed by anyone else is refused.

items.title: Install
items.text:
From the GitHub release of your Lilac, download LilacSonyBridge.apk and bridge.sh. Connect the phone, then on the computer:

  1. Check the phone first. Nothing is changed:

    bash bridge.sh check

    It reports cacao: found (Sony's slow-motion service and its libraries) and raw19 shim: found (the RAW shim Pro mode needs).

  2. Install, always naming the downloaded APK:

    bash bridge.sh install LilacSonyBridge.apk

    The script checks the phone again, copies the APK into place and reboots.

  3. Check again after the reboot. The package line should show /system/priv-app/LilacSonyBridge/, and the flags PRIVILEGED. The request forwarder line says on and names the Lilac it serves once Lilac is installed; if Lilac was installed after the reboot, open it once first (that is when Lilac connects to the bridge).

  4. In Lilac, switch to Video and swipe down on the picture: a Slow-mo switch appears. See slow motion. The new frame rates and stabilisers appear in the everyday row.

items.title: Without adb: a root file browser
items.text:
If you have root on the phone but not rooted adb, you can do by hand what bridge.sh install does. This has not been tried on the phone.

  • Prepare: download LilacSonyBridge.apk as above. A copy of the bridge installed as a normal app hides the system copy, so uninstall it first if you have one (Settings › Apps).
  • Check the ROM: these files must exist, /system/lib64/libcacao_client.so and /system/lib64/libimageprocessorjni.so (Sony's slow-motion service) and /vendor/lib/hw/camera.lilac-real.so (the RAW shim, only for Pro).
  • Unlock: in the file browser, give it root and mount /system read-write (most have a switch for this).
  • Place: create the folder /system/priv-app/LilacSonyBridge and copy the APK into it under exactly the name LilacSonyBridge.apk.
  • Permissions: set the file's permissions to rw-r--r-- (644), owned by root. The script also sets the SELinux label u:object_r:system_file:s0, which a file browser cannot; a file made inside that folder normally gets it anyway. If the bridge does not work after the reboot, check the label first (ls -Z).
  • Reboot: mount /system read-only again if the browser asks, then reboot. Android picks up system apps only at boot.
  • Check: run the checks in step 3 above with normal adb, or look for Lilac Sony Bridge in Settings › Apps with system apps shown. Then do step 4.

items.title: What the warnings mean
items.text: cacao: missing … Slow motion will not work without it. The ROM does not have Sony's slow-motion service or its libraries. The bridge cannot help on this ROM; the script asks Install anyway? [y/N] and stops unless you type y. raw19 shim: missing … Pro mode needs it for RAW. The ROM has no RAW shim. Slow motion does not need it, but Pro mode will not be available. Type y to install anyway. Could not check the phone; nothing was changed. adb could not reach the phone. Check the cable, USB debugging and Rooted debugging, then try again. The script never reports "missing" when it simply could not check.

items.title: Undo
items.text:
bash bridge.sh uninstall

This deletes the bridge's folder and reboots. Lilac keeps working; the Slow-mo switch, the extra frame rates, Steady and Active, and the Lilac Camera entry for other apps disappear.

If you built from source, use sonybridge/tools/bridge.sh and your own sonybridge-debug.apk with a debug-signed Lilac.

items.title: ROM integration (lilac maintainers)
items.text: This page is for maintainers of ROMs for the Xperia XZ1 Compact (lilac) who want to ship Lilac Camera, with 960 fps slow motion, as part of the ROM.

items.title: What you ship
items.text:
Prebuilt APKs from a stable Lilac release (the one marked Latest; pre-releases are betas), imported as they are. Either both apps, or only the bridge:

App Package Installed to Why Lilac Camera io.github.lilaccamera /system/app the camera (optional) Lilac Sony Bridge io.github.lilaccamera.sonybridge /system/priv-app reaches Sony's slow-motion service for Lilac, and passes other apps' photo and video requests to it

Lilac cannot be built in the ROM tree (it is a Gradle build with Compose and its own native libraries), so both come in as prebuilts. With only the bridge, users install Lilac from GitHub and get the same features.

items.title: Importing them
items.text:
Keep the release signatures (presigned); do not re-sign either APK. The bridge trusts Lilac by the certificate of the project's releases, pinned in the bridge, not by the key the bridge itself is signed with. Users update the ROM's copies from later releases like any app, without waiting for a new ROM build. A newer Lilac works with an older bridge: the interface between them only grows, and Lilac uses only what the installed bridge offers.

Android.bp
android_app_import {
    name: "LilacCamera",
    apk: "LilacCamera.apk",
    // keeps the release signature, so later releases install over it
    presigned: true,
    dex_preopt: {
        enabled: true,
    },
}

android_app_import {
    name: "LilacSonyBridge",
    apk: "LilacSonyBridge.apk",
    presigned: true,
    // installs to /system/priv-app
    privileged: true,
    dex_preopt: {
        enabled: true,
    },
}
device.mk
PRODUCT_PACKAGES += \
    LilacCamera \
    LilacSonyBridge

For the bridge alone, leave out the LilacCamera module and its line in PRODUCT_PACKAGES.

  • No privapp-permissions XML is needed. The bridge asks for no privileged permission; it only uses the signature permission it declares itself.
  • Do not sign either app with the platform key. Lilac does not need platform rights.

items.title: What the ROM must already have
items.text:
Lilac does not bring any of Sony's or the shim's files. Do not copy them from another ROM or firmware: a mismatched set can break the camera.

Lilac fully works on sunplex07's LineageOS 23.2 only. Other lilac ROMs get basic multi-frame stacking, because they lack the raw19 camera shim and Sony's cacao service.

Feature Needs on the ROM Tested on Photo, Night, Portrait, Video: multi-frame stacking any lilac ROM, Android 11 or newer Sony's faces, subject tracking, laser focus and camera key Sony's camera driver; expected on any lilac ROM sunplex07's LineageOS 23.2 only Pro (RAW): GCam's HDR+ and HDRNet the raw19 camera shim sunplex07's LineageOS 23.2 960 fps slow motion, 60 and 120 fps video, Sony's stabilisers Sony's cacao service and the Lilac Sony Bridge sunplex07's LineageOS 23.2 only
  • raw19 shim: it wraps Sony's camera HAL as /vendor/lib/hw/camera.lilac-real.so. Ask the shim's author about it. Without it, Pro does not appear in Lilac.
  • cacao: Sony's photo service from the stock vendor image, cacaoserver running as binder service cacao, with /system/lib64/libcacao_client.so and /system/lib64/libimageprocessorjni.so. Without it, the Slow-mo switch does not appear.

items.title: What a system install adds
items.text:
• Capture requests from other apps. Since Android 11, an app that asks the system to take a photo or video (a messenger's camera button, for example) is only offered camera apps that came with the system. As a system app, Lilac answers those requests with its own capture screen. With only the bridge, the bridge takes those requests and passes them to a Lilac installed from GitHub, so it is offered as "Lilac Camera" all the same; the bridge does this only while Lilac is installed as an ordinary app, so a system Lilac is never listed twice.
  • Default camera. You can make Lilac the default camera, or replace the ROM's camera with it.
  • Compiled from the first start. Dexpreopt compiles Lilac at build time. A sideloaded release runs uncompiled until Android compiles it in the background (or adb shell cmd package compile -m speed -f io.github.lilaccamera).

items.title: Checking a build
items.text:
On the built ROM, with adb:

adb shell pm path io.github.lilaccamera.sonybridge
adb shell "dumpsys package io.github.lilaccamera.sonybridge | grep -E 'privateFlags|IMAGE_PROCESSOR'"
adb shell service check cacao

Expected: the path is under /system/priv-app/LilacSonyBridge/, the flags include PRIVILEGED, the permission com.sonymobile.permission.IMAGE_PROCESSOR is listed, and Service cacao: found. On a debug-capable build, bridge.sh check from the release runs the same checks, looks for the shim, and reports the bridge's interface version, whether it passes on photo and video requests, and which Lilac it serves.

Then in Lilac: Video mode, swipe down on the picture, and the Slow-mo switch is there.

items.title: Photo editor
items.text:
Open a photo in the viewer and tap Edit in the action row. The button waits while a photo is still processing.

Lilac's photo editor on the Xperia XZ1 Compact The editor, numbered as in the key below: 1 cancel, undo and redo; 2 HD preview, full view, compare and Save; 3 the photo; 4 the ruler for the chosen setting, on the photo's bottom edge; 5 the settings of the chosen section with their values; 6 the sections. HD Save +0.3 +0.3 Exposure 0 Contrast −12 Highlights +8 Shadows 0 Tonality Look Light Color Effects Detail Portrait Crop 1 2 3 4 5 6 The photo editor on the Xperia XZ1 Compact, to scale.
  1. Cancel, undo, redo
  2. HD preview, full view, compare (hold) and Save. These fade while your finger is on the photo or a ruler.
  3. The photo. Tap it for a full view; long-press it to see the original.
  4. The ruler for the chosen setting, on the photo's bottom edge. Drag it with one finger.
  5. The section's settings with their values. An amber dot marks a changed one; long-press one to see the photo without it.
  6. Sections. Portrait and Crop sit after a small gap; a dot marks a section you changed.

items.title: Around the screen
items.text:
• Sections along the bottom: Look, Light, Color, Effects, Detail, Portrait, Crop. A dot marks a section you changed. Videos have no Portrait or Crop.
  • HD: full-size preview while editing; slower. Without it the preview uses small copies, and Save is still full size.
  • Tap a setting's name for a one-line explanation.

items.title: The sections
items.text:
• Look: the look (LUT) and its intensity, a frame, and presets. Copy edits and Paste edits carry your edits to another photo. Save into look stores the adjustments in the look itself, so every photo using it changes.
  • Light: exposure, contrast, highlights, shadows, tonality and tone curves. Pro photos get Whites, Blacks and a RAW group.
  • Color: temperature, tint, saturation, vibrance; Mixer works by colour, Grading by brightness, Calibration on the camera's red, green and blue.
  • Effects: grain, vignette, fade, bloom, halation, soft light, flash, bleach, fringe and noise.
  • Detail: sharpness, clarity, noise reduction, colour noise and AI denoise.
  • Portrait: the blur, see Portrait.
  • Crop: shape, straighten (up to 45°), turn and flip.

items.title: Pro photos are developed again
items.text:
A Pro photo keeps its RAW file, so the editor develops the RAW again with your changes: a preview first, the full size when you save. Under Light › RAW you choose the rendering engine, colour profile (including imported DCP profiles), lens shading and the base look.

Dynamic range › Re-render rebuilds Lilac's HDR tone map from the RAW.

This changes the photo itself. To try settings without touching it, use Re-render as a copy from the gallery instead (see Pro mode).

items.title: AI denoise
items.text:
Detail › AI denoise runs a neural network that rebuilds detail. It downloads its model (about 47 MB) the first time. It runs on a small preview copy first, then on the whole photo when you save.

Warning

AI denoise is heavy for this phone. If a saved result looks wrong, turn it off and use Noise reduction instead.

items.title: Focus and faces
items.text: Lilac focuses the way Sony's own camera app does: it hands the work to the camera's own subject tracking and face detection, and adds a few rules for this phone's weak spots.

items.title: Tap to focus
items.text:
On the back camera a tap does more than focus on a point:

  • Tap an object: Sony's tracking locks on to it, and the focus mark follows it as it moves. Exposure follows too. Tap it again to go back to automatic.
  • Tap a face frame: that face becomes the main face.
  • Tap nothing in particular, such as a plain wall or a dark area: Lilac notices the tracking has nothing to hold and focuses on the spot you tapped instead.

The focus frame is a thin square: white while focusing, green with a short tick when focus locks, three white blinks on a miss. It fades 1.5 s later.

A tapped point clears itself about 11 s after the last tap or focus result. To keep focus or exposure fixed for longer, set them by hand among the manual values.

The front camera has fixed focus, so a tap only sets the exposure.

items.title: The camera key
items.text:
On the XZ1 Compact's two-stage camera key, a half-press locks focus and exposure on the tracked object or the main face, or the centre if there is neither, for as long as you hold it. An amber AE-L mark shows that exposure is held.

Letting go during a burst waits until the burst has finished.

The volume buttons can shoot too (the default), or step the zoom or the exposure instead: see Buttons on the side.

items.title: Focus in dim light
items.text:
The camera finds focus by looking for contrast. In dim light a small area has too little to go on. So:

  • From ISO 1600 any small focus area (a tap, a small face, the half-press centre) is grown to a fifth of the frame around its centre. A half-press on a far background went from missing to focusing in about 1.5 s.
  • On a miss with nothing near: the back camera has a small laser that measures distance in the middle of the frame, up to about 2 m. When focus fails, the target is in that middle zone and the laser sees nothing near, Lilac sets the lens to its hyperfocal distance (about 4.3 m), which keeps everything from about 2 m to infinity sharp. Any new tap, a laser reading or a scene change hands focus back to the camera.
  • After two misses in a row Lilac stops starting new searches on its own, so the picture does not keep pumping in and out. A tap, a new face or a change of subject starts again.

Lower resolutions also focus faster: see Photo and Night.

items.title: Faces
items.text:
Two face detectors work together.

In the camera In the app Runs on Sony's camera chip, every frame, free the phone's processor, a small neural network Finds up to five faces, a box and a score each faces and the line of the eyes, upright faces only Cost none 55 to 130 ms each time

Lilac uses the camera's faces for nearly everything, because they cost nothing:

  • Face frames, focus and exposure follow the camera's boxes. A face keeps its frame for a moment after it is lost, so frames do not flicker.
  • Smile shutter uses Sony's smile score, 0 to 100 for each face.
  • The self-timer lamp blinks while a face is in view.
  • Portrait's viewfinder keeps a sharp area around each of the camera's faces.

The app's own detector is called only when it adds something:

  • on a tap that missed the camera's faces, to check whether you tapped a face,
  • twice a second while an object is tracked,
  • on a half-press with nothing selected, for up to 0.4 s,
  • for Portrait, to find the line of the eyes,
  • for Human Eye AF (Settings › Lens, off by default), which focuses on a steady eye.

Turning the phone sideways is fine: the app turns the picture upright before it looks.

items.title: Metering
items.text: Metering in quick settings decides which part of the frame sets the exposure: Auto (the camera decides), Centre, Spot (a small circle that follows your tap; drag it to meter elsewhere), Avg (the whole frame) or High (keeps bright areas from turning white).

items.title: Gallery and viewer
items.text: The gallery is the grid of your photos and videos; the viewer is one photo or video full screen. Both are black, take the whole screen and turn with the phone when auto-rotate is on (the camera and the editor stay upright).

items.title: Opening them
items.text:
• The camera's thumbnail opens the viewer on the photo that is still processing, otherwise on the newest photo or video. The picture grows out of the thumbnail and shrinks back into it when you return. With nothing to show, it opens the grid.
  • Swipe down in the viewer for the grid, swipe up for the camera. If a stack is still processing, Lilac asks before it opens the camera (see Exposure bracketing).
  • Optional second icon: Settings › Setup › Interface has a switch (off by default) that adds a Lilac Gallery launcher icon. It opens straight to the grid without starting the camera.

items.title: The grid
items.text:
One line floats over the grid: back, the Lilac and System tabs, and the render queue (with a count, or a mark when something failed). Photos fade out under it.

  • Lilac holds what Lilac made or took in. System shows other apps' photos and videos: they are only viewed, and stay in the phone's gallery.
  • Swipe sideways to go to the other tab. Each tab keeps its scroll place.
  • Tags at the bottom left of a tile, at most two, in the viewer's words: RAW, ×N (versions), ME ×N (multiple exposure), BURST n, LIVE, the video's length, 120 FPS or 960 FPS, IMPORT, LILAC (on the System tab), a lock for a protected photo, and FAILED in red.
  • A tile's edge shows processing, as the thumbnail's does: an arc runs while it renders, dots while it waits, and the picture is dimmed and slightly blurred while it is busy. See the render queue.
  • The date pill and a slim bar show while you scroll fast. A landscape grid has five columns.

items.title: Selecting
items.text:
Long-press a photo, then tap more. A photo that is still processing cannot be selected; a long press says why. A floating row takes the action: Export, Share, Paste look, Delete and Re-render. An action that cannot apply is dimmed and says why.

On the System tab the first action is Add to Lilac: it copies the photos into Lilac's library, skipping any already there. A copy can be rendered again, kept as versions, rated and protected; a system photo can only be viewed.

items.title: Delete has an Undo
items.text: A deleted photo disappears at once and an Undo banner shows for 5 seconds. The files go after that, when you leave the viewer or Lilac goes to the background. A sheet appears only when there is a choice: this version or all, this frame or the whole burst, or exported copies. Protected photos are skipped. Another app's photo goes to the system trash, and Undo asks Android to restore it.

items.title: The viewer
items.text:
Three rows sit over the picture, with no background. Tap the picture to hide them.

  • Top row: the grid icon, a short count while you page, the rating and the photo's tags. A tag explains itself when tapped; LIVE plays, BURST opens the burst and HDR opens its strength.
  • Item row: the version strip, the burst strip or the video timeline, and the processing line.
  • Action row: Camera, Share, Edit, Delete, More.

Double-tap zooms to one pixel of the preview per screen pixel, at the tapped point. In landscape the rows move to the edges: the actions as a column on the right, the top row on the left, and the picture stays centred.

items.title: Versions, bursts and processing
items.text:
• Versions: a Pro photo and its re-rendered copies form one tile. The strip switches between them; the original reads ORIG. The edge of a version's tile shows its state.
  • Bursts: the strip shows the burst's frames and the cover has a star. More offers Use as cover, Export of the shown frame and Export all frames. Edit works on the cover.
  • Processing line: a ring or an icon, the stage, one action and a link to the queue: Pause while rendering, Resume when paused, Retry when it failed, Render for a skipped photo and Render now for one that waits. Render now puts it next, after the render already running.

items.title: Rating and protecting
items.text: The star button adds a star per tap and clears after five. Protect is a switch in More: it shows a lock tag and refuses deleting the photo in the viewer and in the grid. Both belong to the photo, on every version of a stack.

items.title: More
items.text: More opens a sheet with rows in three groups: This photo, Look and Export. It also holds Info, Shooting info (the exposure line and a histogram above the item row), HDR display and Processing queue. A row that cannot apply says why. HDR display is hidden on a screen with no HDR headroom, since it would look the same.

items.title: Videos
items.text:
A video fills the screen and has Lilac's own controls instead of the system player's. The timeline sits in the item row, play and pause in the middle of the picture, and the ¼× / 1× choice and sound above the timeline. A tap shows or hides the rows.

A 120 fps clip shows its slowed part as a band on the timeline. Drag its ends; it plays at ¼× inside and 1× outside, and the range is kept with the clip.

While a clip is paused, previous frame, Save frame and next frame can appear. Save frame imports the frame as a new photo with the clip's look. They are off by default: turn on Show on the picture in More. Frame step shows only after the clip has played and been paused.

A clip with no look plays straight to the screen. A clip with a look larger than 1080p is scaled down to 1080p before the look is applied, because 4K through the look made this phone's graphics chip fail. A clip that cannot play says so.

items.title: The editor
items.text: Edit opens the editor. The picture glides from its place in the viewer to its place in the editor, and back, unless you are zoomed in or in landscape.

items.title: First launch
items.text:
Lilac asks for the camera and the microphone. On Android 13 and newer it also asks for notifications. They are optional: they only show the progress of Pro photos that finish in the background.

There is no tour. A small pill, How to use Lilac, sits above the shutter in Photo mode until you open it once. It walks through modes, quick settings, manual controls, zoom and looks. To see it again, open quick settings and tap the info mark next to the mode name.

items.title: The camera screen
items.text:
• Top line: small marks for anything switched on or not at its default, such as a timer (3s), Live, Smile, flash or a light reading like 12 lux. Tap them to open the everyday row. Sony's scene icons can appear at the right end.
  • Above the shutter: quick settings on the left, the zoom control (a thumbwheel) in the middle, looks on the right.
  • Bottom row: the latest photo on the left, the shutter with the mode dial in the middle, the camera switch on the right.

Tap the picture to focus and meter there. A long press locks focus. Pinch to zoom.

items.title: Modes
items.text:
Swipe sideways on the shutter to change mode, or tap the faint mode mark beside it. From left to right:

Mode Mark For Night dim scenes; stacks every shot Portrait people, with the background blurred Pro M RAW photos, developed by Lilac Photo AUTO everyday shots Video video

A short flick moves one mode; a slow swipe can cross them all. The dial stops at Night and at Video. It is locked while a video records.

Pro is only on the dial when the camera gives apps RAW frames. On the front camera, or on a ROM without the raw19 shim, the dial has no M.

items.title: Quick settings
items.text:
Tap quick settings . A sheet rises from the bottom; tap the picture or drag the sheet down to close it. Group titles are off by default, to keep the lists short; switch them on with Group titles in Settings.

  • The everyday row on top: Live, timer, Smile, aspect and flash in the photo modes; resolution, frame rate, torch and stabilisation in Video. Tap an item to step to its next value; its value shows inside or beside the icon. You can also swipe down on the picture to show just this row.
  • Below it are two tabs. Shooting holds what changes the shot (Lens, Stacking, Exposure, HDR+ and the mode's own settings), Output what changes the file. Swipe sideways or tap a tab. The same row has the Toolbox, Content management and Settings icons. The front camera has one page and no tabs.
  • Tap a setting's name for a one-line explanation. Long-press it to open the full setting in Settings.

items.title: Symbols on the camera screen
items.text: Symbol Means self-timer (3, 5 or 10 s) Live photo: a short video with the photo Smile shutter: shoots when the face smiles flash on or off torch on or off multi-exposure: several shots in one picture the light reading, such as 12 lux, in dim light Night's Fast or Accurate switch opens the guide for the current mode the phone is warming up while recording

items.title: Manual controls
items.text:
How to use the manual controls

Swipe up on the picture. The values appear along its bottom edge: EV (exposure), Tv (shutter), ISO, AF (focus) and AWB (white balance). Portrait adds Av (blur strength); Night adds Frames.

  • A value on Auto shows the camera's live reading, such as 1/60 or ISO 400.
  • Drag a value sideways to change it. A ruler shows while you drag.
  • Tap a value to keep its ruler open. Tap A on the ruler, or double-tap the value, to go back to Auto.
  • A value you set by hand gets a small amber dot and stays on screen.
  • Focus has an H button for hyperfocal focus.
  • EV only works while exposure is on Auto.
  • Pro opens with the values showing. In other modes they hide about 5 s after your last touch.
  • The front camera has no manual shutter or ISO. Tapping them says "Not available on this camera".

items.title: Zoom
items.text:
Turn the thumbwheel above the shutter with your thumb: its rim follows your finger, holds for a moment at each stop with a tick, coasts after a flick, and a tap on a number goes there. While you zoom the note line shows the zoom and its 35 mm focal length. Pinching reaches the full range.

In Settings › Setup › Interface, Zoom control can be changed to a simple pill (the same, with a white disc) or the collar: a curved band that zooms faster the harder you pull it sideways, left to zoom in, and springs back. Tap T or W on the collar to step, or hold them to keep zooming. With Volume Key Action set to Focal Switch, the volume buttons step the zoom too (see Buttons on the side).

items.title: Buttons on the side
items.text:
The XZ1 Compact's side buttons work as camera controls, so you can shoot without reaching across the screen:

  • Camera key, half-press: focuses and holds focus and exposure while you keep it there. See Focus and faces.
  • Camera key, full press: takes the photo, or starts and stops a video. During a slow-motion recording it fires the 960 fps burst.
  • Volume buttons: take the photo by default. In Settings › Setup › Controls › Volume Key Action you can make them Focal Switch (zoom: up steps in, down steps out, one stop at a time, like tapping T or W), Exposure Comp. (up brightens, down darkens) or Volume Control (they change the volume as usual).

items.title: Looks
items.text:
A look is a colour style (a LUT). Swipe sideways on the picture to step through your favourite looks. Tap for all of them, with Intensity, colour recipe, frame and presets. A Manage tile at the end of the strip opens content management.

In Night that button becomes Night's Fast or Accurate switch instead. Looks cannot change while a video records.

items.title: The latest photo
items.text: Tap the thumbnail to open the viewer on the photo still processing, or else the newest photo or video. Its edge shows processing: a running arc while a photo is processed, a dotted ring while photos wait, pause bars when processing is paused, and an amber ring when Android keeps stopping a Pro photo for memory. See Pro mode.

items.title: Sony camera features
items.text: Lilac aims to bring everything Sony's own camera app does to custom ROMs, and to add GCam's multi-frame processing on top. Sony's camera software publishes more than Android's standard camera interface shows, and Lilac uses the parts it can reach. This page lists what is done and what is not.

items.title: Sony's camera app and Lilac
items.text:
Sony's camera In Lilac Face detection Done. Light face frames on both cameras; focus and exposure follow the main face Subject tracking Done. Tap an object and it is followed (back camera) Focus and exposure marks, the half-press Done. Sony-style focus frame, metering circle, AE-L Laser distance sensor Partly. A far-focus fallback in the dark Two-stage camera key Done. Half-press holds focus, full press shoots Smile shutter Done Scene and condition recognition Partly. Icons on the top line; nothing changes because of them Sony's photo processing Done on the front camera, as Accurate colour; Camera JPEG keeps Sony's photo in Pro Super slow motion, 960 fps Done, at 720p. Needs Sony's cacao service and the Lilac Sony Bridge on the ROM 60 fps at 1080p and 120 fps at 720p video Done. Needs Sony's cacao service and the Lilac Sony Bridge Still HDR By hand. Only as a custom vendor key Multi-frame noise reduction Not used. Lilac merges the frames itself Video stabilisation (SteadyShot, Intelligent Active) Done, as Steady and Active. Needs the Lilac Sony Bridge; Lilac's own EIS+ works without it

What each ROM provides, and which ROM was tested: Get Lilac.

items.title: The phone's cameras
items.text:
Back Front Sensor Sony IMX400, 19 MP (5056 × 3792) 8 MP (3264 × 2448) RAW yes, through the raw19 shim no Manual ISO and shutter yes, ISO 50 to 3200 no Focus autofocus with a laser distance sensor fixed Stabilisation none in the lens none Flash LED the screen lights the face

Above ISO 320 the back sensor's gain is digital rather than analog.

items.title: What Lilac uses
items.text:
The camera's own features that Lilac uses, in detail. Open on a card to see what each one does in the app.

Face detectionOn the camera chip, up to five faces, at no cost to the phone.What it does in Lilac

Lilac draws the face frames and points focus and exposure at faces. Portrait keeps a sharp area round each face in the viewfinder, and the self-timer lamp blinks while a face is in view. See Faces.

Subject trackingBack camera: the camera follows an object as it moves.What it does in Lilac

Tap an object and the focus mark follows it as it moves, with the exposure. A half-press of the camera key locks on to it. See Tap to focus.

Focus areaThe camera focuses on the area the app gives it.What it does in Lilac

Focus goes where you tap. In dim light Lilac makes a small area bigger, so the camera has enough contrast to focus. See Focus in dim light.

Exposure on facesThe camera meters on the faces it finds.What it does in Lilac

Faces come out well exposed without tapping them. See Faces.

Laser distance sensorBack camera: measures distance in the middle of the frame, up to about 2 m.What it does in Lilac

When focus fails in the dark and the laser sees nothing near, Lilac sets the lens so everything from about 2 m to infinity is sharp. See Focus in dim light.

Smile scoresHow much each face smiles, 0 to 100.What it does in Lilac

Smile shutter takes a photo each time the main face smiles enough. See Smile shutter.

Still processingSony's full photo pipeline, with the true black level.What it does in Lilac

The front camera's Accurate colour, in Photo, Portrait and Night, removes the pink cast from dim shadows. In Pro, Camera JPEG keeps Sony's own photo to compare with. See Front camera colour.

Two-stage camera keyA half-press and a full press, like a compact camera.What it does in Lilac

A half-press focuses and holds focus and exposure; a full press takes the photo or starts and stops a video; during slow motion it fires the burst. See Buttons on the side.

Super slow motion serviceSony's cacao service records 960 frames a second (ROM support needed).What it does in Lilac

Video mode's Slow-mo switch records a 960 fps burst at 720p that plays back in slow motion. See Slow motion.

items.title: Scene and condition detection
items.text:
Sony's camera recognises the scene and how the phone is held. Lilac shows these icons at the right end of the top line. They only inform; Lilac changes nothing because of them.

Backlight Night Low light Landscape Portrait Document Food Spotlight Macro Tripod Walking Motion

From the phone: the gyroscope (the steadiest frame, Night's shake plan), the light sensor (the Night offer), the flash LED and the vibrator.

items.title: Vendor keys
items.text:
Android apps talk to the camera through Camera2, a standard set of controls such as exposure time, ISO and focus. A camera's software can add its own controls on top, called vendor keys, with names like com.sonymobile.control.afRegionMode. They are not documented. An app finds them in the lists the camera reports, and has to know each key's type and values.

They are risky: a key the camera does not accept, or a wrong value, makes the camera refuse the request, and Android closes the camera. So Lilac sends each Sony key only to a camera that lists it. The front camera, for one, closes on the laser key.

The Sony keys Lilac uses Key (com.sonymobile.…) For statistics.objectSelectTrigger, objectSelectTriggerArea start and stop subject tracking at a tap statistics.objectSelectArea where the tracked subject is statistics.faceSelectTrigger, faceSelectArea choose the main face control.aeRegionMode = face exposure follows faces control.afRegionMode = user focus on the app's area statistics.tofMeasureMode, tofMeasureArea the laser distance reading statistics.faceSmileScoresMode, faceSmileScores smile scores statistics.sceneDetectMode, scene, conditionDetectMode, condition scene and condition icons Keys found but not used

These exist on the phone, in Sony's own camera app, but Lilac does not use them: still HDR (control.stillHdrMode), Sony's ISO and shutter hints, a power-save mode for heat, skin smoothing, Sony's distortion correction (it did nothing in this camera path), an amber-blue colour nudge, the colour-of-light sensor, Sony's own exposure modes (meanings unknown), and dual-camera controls (this phone has one back camera).

items.title: Custom vendor keys
items.text:
Settings › Lens › Camera2 Extensions › Custom Vendor Keys lets you add a key yourself: its full name, whether it goes on each request (Capture key) or on the camera session (Session key), its type (int32 or u8), the value and the lens (0 is the back camera, 1 the front).

For example, Sony's still HDR: com.sonymobile.control.stillHdrMode, Capture key, u8, value 1, lens 0. In a test it about halved the blown-out area, on automatic exposure only, at the cost of about a third of a stop of light, and did nothing for the shadows.

Warning

A key the camera does not accept stops the camera. If it will not open after you add a key, delete the key and restart the app.

items.title: What Lilac does not reach
items.text: Sony's own photo and video service (it does Sony's multi-frame noise reduction, slow motion and SteadyShot video) only talks to privileged system apps. Lilac reaches it only for slow motion, through a separate bridge app the ROM must ship.

items.title: HDR
items.text: A bright window and a dark room can be seven stops apart: one is 128 times brighter than the other. No single exposure holds both. HDR in Lilac means keeping the bright parts from turning white and lifting the dark parts, without the flat, grey look of heavy HDR.

items.title: Two ways to keep a window
items.text:
A window that is white in a frame stays white, however many frames you merge: merging lowers noise, but it cannot bring back what was never recorded. So Lilac changes the exposure before it shoots, in two different ways:

  • Photo mode: exposure bracketing. Next to the normal frames it takes one darker and one brighter frame, and fuses the three.
  • Pro: the darker burst. Every frame of the RAW burst is shot darker, and the merge averages the noise away.

Which one to use, and why they differ: Bracketing or a darker burst.

items.title: Exposure bracketing
items.text:
Bracketing is a Photo mode setting: the multi-frame stack gets two extra shots at other exposures, so bright skies and dark shadows both keep detail. It is on by default for new installs.

Switch it with Bracketing in quick settings (Shooting tab, next to Multi-frame), or in Settings › Photo. When it cannot be used, the row says why (see When it is off).

items.title: What one press does
items.text:
1. Lilac looks at the viewfinder and picks how far to go: the more of it is white, the darker the dark frame; the more of it is black, the brighter the bright frame.
  2. It shoots the normal frames (the Multi-frame count, 5 by default), one darker frame and one brighter frame. With 5 frames that is 7 shots.
  3. The normal frames are stacked, as in any Photo shot, which lowers their noise.
  4. The stack, the dark frame and the bright frame are fused: for each part of the picture, the fusion takes the frame where it is best exposed. Windows come from the dark frame, shadows from the bright one, the rest from the stack.
White in the viewfinder Dark frame Black in the viewfinder Bright frame under 0.5 % 1 stop darker under 5 % 1 stop brighter 0.5 to 2 % 1.5 stops 5 to 15 % 2 stops 2 to 5 % 2 stops 15 to 30 % 2.5 stops 5 % or more 2.5 stops 30 % or more 3 stops

The bright frame is not allowed a long shutter, so it is not blurred by shake: its shutter stays at 1/100 s or shorter, and ISO makes up the rest. Hold the phone very steady and it may go longer.

items.title: When it is off
items.text:
• Back camera only. The front camera has no manual exposure, so its extra frames would come out the same as the others.
  • Needs Multi-frame. With Multi-frame off there is no stack to add to.
  • 12 MP or 8 MP, not full size. A bracketed stack at 19 MP runs a 4 GB phone out of memory, so at full size the row reads "12 MP or less" and the switch does nothing. Photo mode starts at 12 MP.
  • Photo mode only. Night plans its own frames, and Pro uses the darker burst.

If you go back from the gallery to the camera while a stack is still being fused, Lilac asks first ("Photo still processing"): opening the camera now may run the phone out of memory. The photo is safe either way. Stay in the gallery, go to the home screen, or open the camera anyway.

items.title: Bracketing or a darker burst
items.text:
Both keep what a normal exposure loses to white. They get there differently:

Photo: exposure bracketing Pro: the darker burst Frames 3 different exposures: normal (several), darker, brighter all the same exposure, darker by 1 to 3 stops Made from Sony's finished 8-bit frames RAW, before Sony's processing Highlights come from the one dark frame every frame Shadows come from the bright frame and the stack the merge: averaging many dark, noisy frames Joined by exposure fusion, which picks the best-exposed parts of each frame merge, then tone mapping lifts the shadows (capped by the HDR ratio) Extra frames 2 none; the whole burst is darker Time and memory light at 12 MP; Photo mode's own speed slow, 15 to 22 s for 13 frames; heavy, about 1 GB Camera back back

The difference in one line: bracketing measures the shadows with a brighter frame; the darker burst measures them with many dark frames and averages the noise out.

So a bracketed Photo shot is quick and handles an ordinary contrast, such as a sunny street with shade. It has only one dark frame to hold the highlights and one bright frame for the shadows, both taken from Sony's already-processed picture. The darker burst has far more data in the shadows and the highlights, because it starts from RAW and merges many frames. In Lilac's tests only a darker Pro burst held a scene as hard as a bright window next to a dark room. Use Pro for those, and Photo bracketing for the rest.

Pro also has its own HDR+ bracket exposure (Spatial merge mode only, off by default). That is a third thing, with RAW frames at different exposures; see Pro. It is not worth it on this phone.

items.title: The darker burst
items.text:
In Pro, Lilac checks the viewfinder before a burst. If part of it is already pure white, it shoots the whole burst darker, so the bright parts keep their detail:

White in the viewfinder Burst shot darker by 0.5 % 1 stop 2 % 2 stops 5 % or more 3 stops

Darker frames are noisier in the shadows, but the merge averages that noise away. The tone mapping then lifts the shadows back up. So the highlights come from a dark exposure and the shadows from the merge.

It never goes darker than the frame count can pay back: at most 1 stop for 2 frames, 1.6 for 3, 2 for 4 and 3 for 8 or more. It lowers ISO first and only then shortens the shutter.

It happens by itself when:

  • ISO and shutter are both on Auto,
  • HDR+ frames is 2 or more,
  • the merge mode is Sabre (the default).

items.title: The HDR ratio slider
items.text:
HDR ratio in Pro's quick settings, just under HDR+ frames: 1× to 20×, default 8×. Double-tap it to go back to 8×.

It is a limit, not a strength. Lilac's tone mapping uses Google's learned auto-exposure to decide how many times brighter the shadows may be made than the highlights. The slider caps that ratio.

  • The scene often wants less than the cap. Then raising it changes nothing.
  • Lowering it gives a gentler lift: darker shadows, a more ordinary-looking photo. 4× or 2.5× look like a regular photo.
  • When the cap bites, the difference is shared: shadows are lifted less and highlights brought down less.
  • A big face in the frame lowers the cap, to no less than 6×.

The value in force is saved with each photo, so it applies to new shots. The same setting is HDR Ratio limit in Settings.

items.title: What the photo used
items.text:
Open a Pro photo, then its info. The HDR · ratio 6.8× row expands to:

  • Ratio used: what the tone mapping applied.
  • Scene wanted: what the scene asked for before the limit.
  • Ratio limit: your HDR ratio when the photo was taken.
  • Viewfinder match: how far the brightness was pulled toward the viewfinder picture. Merged bursts keep their own brightness, so this is near 0.

If "Scene wanted" is above "Ratio limit", the slider made a difference.

items.title: Ultra HDR
items.text:
Ultra HDR in quick settings (off by default) adds a gain map, so photos look brighter on HDR screens. The gain map is built from the RAW, so it works for Pro photos. Each photo in the gallery has its own HDR switch and strength.

Sony's own still HDR can only be turned on by hand as a vendor key; see Sony camera features.

items.title: How a picture is made
items.text: This page explains what happens between the sensor and the saved photo: which pictures the camera hands to Lilac, how Lilac merges them, and why it works the way it does on a phone with 4 GB of memory.

items.title: Why one frame is not enough
items.text:
A sensor counts light. In dim light, or in the dark parts of any scene, it counts so little that random variation, noise, is a large part of what it records. A bigger lens or sensor would collect more light; a phone cannot have either.

What a phone can do is take several frames and merge them. The scene is the same in every frame; the noise is different each time. Averaging keeps the scene and cancels much of the noise. Lilac calls this stacking.

items.title: The camera's three streams
items.text:
An app does not read the sensor directly. It asks the camera for pictures in a given form, called a stream, and the camera's software decides what reaches it.

Three streams from one sensor The sensor feeds three streams. Sony's image processor gives YUV frames, which Lilac stacks in Photo, Night and Portrait. Sony's still pipeline gives a camera JPEG, used for the front camera's Accurate colour. The raw19 shim gives 10-bit RAW frames, which Lilac merges and develops in Pro. Sensor Sony IMX400 · 19 MP Sony's processor YUV · 30 per second Photo · Night · Portrait stacked by Lilac Sony's still pipeline camera JPEG · slow Front camera colour Accurate mode raw19 shim (ROM) RAW · 10-bit Pro merged and developed the phone's camera Lilac One sensor, three streams. Lilac's work is in the lilac boxes. YUV Camera JPEG RAW What it is Sony's finished frames Sony's full still photo the sensor's own data Processing denoised, sharpened, toned by Sony Sony's whole still pipeline none Depth 8 bits per channel 8 bits, compressed 10 bits, linear Speed up to 30 frames a second slow; the sensor switches mode one full-size frame every 0.44 s Size any size up to 19 MP any size full size only, about 38 MB Available on every ROM on every ROM only with the raw19 shim Lilac uses it for Photo, Night, Portrait front camera Accurate colour, comparison copies Pro

YUV is what most camera apps work from: the same frames that normally become the JPEG, before compression. They are quick and cheap, but Sony has already made its choices: its noise reduction smooths fine detail, and what it crushed to black or clipped to white is gone.

RAW is the sensor's reading before any of that. Sony's camera software on the XZ1 Compact does not offer RAW to apps at all. sunplex07's unofficial LineageOS 23.2 for lilac adds it with the raw19 camera shim, which sits between Android and Sony's camera library. The shim only delivers a full-size RAW frame when the same request also asks for a full-size JPEG, so every Pro frame carries a JPEG that Lilac throws away (or keeps, with Camera JPEG on).

Camera JPEG is Sony's complete still pipeline, as Sony's own app gets it. Lilac uses it where Sony's processing does something no setting can: on the front camera, Sony's still processing removes the sensor's black offset that tints the normal stream pink in dim light. See front camera colour.

items.title: How stacking works
items.text:
The idea is the same in Photo and Pro; the material differs.

The steps of stacking Five steps: take a burst; pick the steadiest frame as reference; line the other frames up with it tile by tile; merge each pixel, averaging frames that agree and leaving out those where something moved; the result is one photo with the same brightness and much less noise. 1 Take a burstframes a moment apart 2 Pick a referencethe steadiest frame, by gyroscope 3 Line the frames uptile by tile, small shifts 4 Merge each pixelagrees: averaged in; moved: left out 5 One photosame brightness, much less noise Stacking, step by step.
  1. Burst. One press takes several frames in quick succession.
  2. Reference. One frame is the anchor the others are matched to. In Photo mode it is the steadiest of the first four, read from the gyroscope; in Pro it is the sharpest, judged from the pixels.
  3. Alignment. Hands move between frames, so each frame is split into tiles and every tile is shifted to line up with the reference.
  4. Merge. For each pixel Lilac asks: does this frame agree with the reference, allowing for the noise expected at this brightness? If yes, it is averaged in. If not, something moved there, and the frame counts for less, so moving people do not leave ghosts. The expected noise is measured for each frame, so at high ISO plain noise is not mistaken for movement.
  5. Result. One photo at the brightness of one frame, with much less noise.

items.title: Photo mode: stacking the processed stream
items.text:
Photo mode stacks YUV frames on the phone's graphics chip, with all frames in memory at once. A burst at 30 frames a second is over quickly, so it works handheld and with people.

It starts from Sony's processing, so it inherits it: Sony's noise reduction leaves coarse colour blotches that stacking reduces less than grain, and detail Sony already smoothed or crushed does not come back.

items.title: Pro: stacking RAW
items.text:
Pro stacks RAW frames before anything has touched them:

  • Linear data. RAW values are proportional to the light, so frames add up exactly, like photon counts.
  • A noise model of this sensor. Lilac uses a noise profile measured on the XZ1 Compact, so it knows how much of each pixel is noise at each brightness. The profile the shim reports is about twice too high and would make the merge throw away good detail.
  • Processing once, at the end. GCam's denoising, exposure and tone mapping, then Lilac's colour and look, run on one clean frame instead of many noisy ones; see what comes from GCam.

The cost is speed: each RAW frame is a full-size still, so a burst needs a steadier hand or a support; see HDR+ frames.

items.title: How many frames
items.text:
Averaging N frames leaves 1/√N of the noise. Each extra frame helps less than the one before:

Noise left after stacking Noise falls with the square root of the frame count: 58 % at 3 frames, 45 % at 5, 32 % at 10, 22 % at 20. Tripod measurements match it: 58 to 62 % at 3 frames, 20 to 34 % at 20. most of the gain 0% 25% 50% 75% 100% 1 5 10 15 20 1 frames: 100 % of the noise left 3 frames: 58 % of the noise left 5 frames: 45 % of the noise left 10 frames: 32 % of the noise left 20 frames: 22 % of the noise left 3 frames, measured on a tripod: 58 to 62 % 20 frames, measured on a tripod: 20 to 34 % √N law frames merged √N law measured on a tripod Noise left after merging, compared with a single frame. Hover a point for its value. The numbers behind the chart Frames Noise left (√N law) Measured on a tripod 1 100 % 3 58 % 58 to 62 % 5 45 % 10 32 % 20 22 % 20 to 34 %

Measured in Photo mode at 12 MP, ISO 800 and ISO 3200, each stack against its own single frame.

  • On a tripod Lilac reaches the law: the merge keeps nearly every frame.
  • Handheld, shake and movement cost frames: a gently shaken 12-frame burst was worth about 8.
  • 5 to 10 frames give most of the gain. Beyond about 12 handheld, blur from a longer burst grows faster than noise falls.
  • Night goes further: it also brightens, by up to √N, so more frames allow more brightening without more noise.

items.title: Keeping bright skies and windows
items.text:
A merge lowers noise, but cannot bring back light that was never recorded. If a window is white in every frame, it is white in the result. So in Pro Lilac changes the exposure before it shoots:

How a darker burst keeps a bright window Illustration on a scale of seven stops from a dark room to a bright window. One frame at normal exposure loses the window to white. A burst shot three stops darker keeps the window but its shadows are noisy. Merging thirteen frames removes most of that noise, so the whole scene is kept, and tone mapping lifts the room back up. The scene dark roombright window One frame, normal exposure lost in noise recorded with detail clipped to white the window turns white Each frame of the burst, 3 stops darker lost in noise recorded with detail window kept, the room is noisy 13 frames merged lost in noise recorded with detail noise averaged away; the room is lifted back detail noise white An illustration on a scale of seven stops (each stop doubles the light).

When part of the viewfinder is already white, Lilac shoots the whole burst darker. Each frame then keeps the window but has noisier shadows; merging averages that noise away; the tone mapping lifts the room back up. How much darker, when, and the limits: the darker burst.

How far the shadows may be lifted is capped by the HDR ratio. Photo mode does it differently: its frames are Sony's finished pictures, so instead of shooting them all darker it adds one darker and one brighter frame and fuses the three. See Exposure bracketing, which also explains how that differs from the darker burst.

items.title: Memory on a 4 GB phone
items.text:
Merging needs every frame in memory at once, and developing a RAW needs about 1 GB. On a 4 GB phone shared with Android and other apps, often only 0.5 to 1.5 GB is free.

Memory needed against memory free A 20-frame stack needs about 575 MB at 19 MP, 240 MB at 12 MP and 58 MB for the 2 MP front camera. Developing one RAW needs about 1 GB. A 4 GB phone often has only 500 to 1500 MB free. often free 20 frames, 19 MP Photo stack at full size: about 575 MB 575 MB 20 frames, 12 MP Photo stack at 12 MP: about 240 MB 240 MB 20 frames, front 2 MP front-camera stack: about 58 MB 58 MB one RAW develop Pro, one 19 MP photo: about 1000 MB 1 GB 0 500 1000 1500 MB Memory needed, against what is often free. Hover a bar for details.

That shapes the design:

  • 12 MP on the back camera in Photo mode needs less than half the memory of full size, and is the default. Bracketing needs it. See resolution.
  • 2 MP on the front camera uses the sensor's own 2 × 2 pixel binning: less noise, a quarter of the memory.
  • Pro photos are developed one at a time, in their own process, which waits for enough free memory and saves its progress. Closing the app frees its graphics memory for the render. See the render queue.

items.title: From press to photo
items.text:
What happens after you press Photo: a burst of frames 1/30 s apart, merged on the graphics chip, saved within seconds. Pro single frame: the RAW is saved at once; about 5 s after the last shot, and once enough memory is free, a separate process develops it into the photo. Pro burst: frames 0.44 s apart, merged and developed in the camera, 15 to 22 s for 13 frames. Photo burst1/30 s apart mergegraphics chip savedseconds Pro, 1 frame RAW savedat once waitsfor free memory developedown process Pro burst burst0.44 s apart mergeand develop saved15 to 22 s What happens after you press, in order. Not to scale.
  • Photo: the burst is over in a fraction of a second, the merge runs right after, and the photo is saved within seconds.
  • Pro, one frame: the RAW file is saved at once and developed later in its own process; see the render queue.
  • Pro, burst: hold still for the whole burst; the merge and develop then run in the camera. Timings: HDR+ frames.

items.title: Optimizations and tweaks
items.text:
Lilac started as a fork of PhotonCamera. This page lists what Lilac has changed on its own since then, in three groups: Sony's camera features, GCam's multi-frame processing and the memory work behind it, and the rest of the app. It does not list PhotonCamera's own features.

The measurements were taken on an Xperia XZ1 Compact, a phone with 4 GB of memory and a 4.6-inch screen. Most of the work follows from those two facts, and from the aim of bringing Sony's camera features and GCam's processing to this phone.

Words used on this page RAW The sensor's unprocessed picture data. It holds more detail than a JPEG and is developed afterwards. Stacking (merging) Taking several shots and combining them into one photo with less noise and more detail. Burst Several shots in quick succession. Lilac merges the shots of a burst into one photo. HDR Combining a darker and a brighter shot so that both the bright and the dark parts of a scene keep their detail. Noise The grainy speckle that shows up in dim photos. ISO The camera's light sensitivity. A higher ISO brightens a dim scene and adds more noise. Exposure How much light a photo gets, set by the shutter speed and the ISO. Viewfinder The live picture on the screen while you frame a shot. Frame One picture of a burst or a video. GPU The phone's graphics chip. Lilac uses it for much of the photo processing, and on this phone it has to share its memory with everything else. Look (LUT) A colour style applied to a photo, such as a film look. Bokeh The soft blur behind a subject in a portrait. MP Megapixels, the size of a picture. The phone's back camera takes 19 MP photos.

items.title: Sony camera features
items.text: Lilac's work on Sony's own camera features: face and subject tracking, focus, Sony's photo processing and slow motion. What is done and what is not yet is on Sony camera features.

items.title: Focus, faces and exposure
items.text:
• Sony-style face frames and subject tracking. Up to five faces get a light frame that glides smoothly, and tapping something that is not a face follows that object. Focus and exposure are steered to the tracked face or object, using the phone's own face detection and tracking, as Sony's camera does. (d115118)
  • Half-press on the camera key holds focus and exposure, like a Sony camera. Half-pressing locks focus and exposure on your tapped point or the centre; a point already in focus shows green at once with a light tick, and a miss is focused again. An amber exposure lock mark shows on the top edge. (f9a19ab, a5050a8)
  • Smile shutter. A new Smile tile takes the photo by itself when the main face smiles as much as you set (small, average or big), at most once a second. A gauge on the face frame fills with the smile. Smile and the self-timer switch each other off. (3bd1e2f)
  • Faces are found with the phone held sideways. Eye focus and Portrait no longer lose the face in landscape, on the back and front camera. The viewfinder picture is turned to match the phone's rotation before faces are looked for. (79611ed, 03c9339)
  • A Sony-style focus frame. A tap draws a thin square: white while focusing, green with a light tick when focus locks, three white blinks on a miss. On the front camera, which cannot report focus, a tap now only sets exposure and shows an exposure circle. (c145afa)
  • Metering circle like Sony's. In Spot metering (measuring brightness at one point) a small circle sits in the centre and moves with your tap, and can be dragged elsewhere. Centre-weighted metering shows it fixed in the centre; other modes show none. Starting tracking no longer sends it to the centre first. (f9a19ab, 28b3a75, d9ae10c)
  • A tapped focus point stays put in dim light. Leftover results from the previous focus lock and ongoing brightness changes were mistaken for a scene change, so the point was dropped within about a second. The app now waits for the real focus result and for exposure to settle. (2b19e20, 60b812d)
  • Bigger focus area in dim light. From ISO 1600 up, a small focus area is enlarged, because a tiny dark patch holds too little detail to focus on. In a test, a half-press on a far background went from missing to focusing in about 1.5 s. (825e5db)
  • Subject focus searches are no longer cut short. A search used to be ended early by a leftover "focused" result from before it started, so many were cancelled almost at once. They now wait for their own result, and the time limit grows from 2 s to 4 s so the lens can finish a full sweep. (71576ff)
  • No endless focus hunting in the dark. In a scene too dark to focus, the lens used to sweep its whole range again every 2 s. After two misses in a row, it now stops searching until the subject changes, you tap or choose a face, or continuous focus finds focus again. (bd2c75b)
  • Far subjects the camera cannot focus on get a sensible fallback. If a tap, half-press or subject search ends unfocused and the back camera's laser distance sensor (which sees only to about 2 m) sees nothing, the lens is set so everything from about 2 m outwards is sharp. Automatic focus returns on the next tap or scene change. (4c82b7e)
  • A tap on a plain area focuses on that spot. A blank or dark area has no object to follow, and the tracking box used to wander off. If it drifts or is lost soon after the tap, tracking stops and the tap becomes an ordinary fixed focus point. (3824610)
  • Taps on the front camera land in the right place. The front camera's picture is mirrored, and the app undid the mirroring in the wrong order, so on most front cameras a tap was measured at the opposite point of the picture. It now maps correctly. (f30a417)
  • An old tapped point clears itself. A tapped point is dropped about 10 seconds after its mark fades, so a later half-press starts from the centre again. A point whose brightness you moved away from the focus mark stays until your next tap. (a5050a8)

items.title: Front camera
items.text:
• Choose Fast or Accurate colour on the front camera. In dim light, front camera photos come out violet-magenta with lifted blacks. A new quick settings choice, Accurate, gives true colours by using Sony's own photo processing, at about 4 frames per second, so bursts are slower; Fast keeps 30. The live view is also adjusted to look closer to the photo. (3ca889d, 4e5bfbb, 611065c, 8853928, 9bde3a4, e397c24)
  • The screen lights your face as a flash. The front camera has no flash, so Flash on now turns the screen white and its backlight to full for the shot. The white stays until the whole capture, merged shots included, has ended. It works in Photo and Portrait. (767760f)
  • The front camera starts at 2 MP, with its own size setting. The 2 MP size gives cleaner photos in dim light, while larger front sizes come out with crushed black shadows and garish colours at high sensitivity. Full size is one tap away, and a size you chose earlier is kept. (11794c9, fa73d5e)
  • Night always uses 2 MP on the front camera. Whatever size Photo mode has chosen, Night uses 2 MP, and your choice comes back when you leave Night. Quick settings show it as a fixed 2 MP. (ccc58a4)
  • No more brightness flicker at full size. On the front camera in Photo mode at full size, the live view's brightness no longer swings several times a second. The app sends one small focus nudge just after the preview starts and puts focus back after about a second. (104c2af, 3b36edd)
  • Switching to a camera without manual exposure no longer freezes the readings. After going from a camera with manual ISO and shutter to one without, such as the front camera, the other camera froze its readings and greyed out exposure adjustment until restart. Such a camera now always meters automatically. (68999a6)

items.title: Video and slow motion
items.text:
• 960 frames per second slow motion. On the Xperia XZ1 Compact the app can now record Sony's super slow motion. Sony's photo service only talks to a privileged system app, so a small companion app does the recording and Lilac talks to it. Only Lilac may use it. (20ddd3e, d2f30f4)
  • 60 fps at 1080p and 120 fps at 720p. With the Lilac Sony Bridge, Video offers two more frame rates through Sony's own video mode. Lilac draws the frames itself, so looks, sound and Pause work as in normal video, and 120 fps files carry the rate so other apps read them correctly. (b4cae10, ffe5eca, 0683bea, 2b7e64d)
  • Sony's video stabilisers. Stabilise now steps through Off, EIS+, Steady (SteadyShot) and Active (Intelligent Active), offering each only at the sizes and rates where it works. (adccee5)
  • The gallery plays 120 fps videos slowed. A 120 fps video opens four times slower, with a switch to full speed, and Share and Export ask Slowed or Full speed. (1101088, 585f630)
  • Slow-mo switch and burst button. In Video mode a Slow-mo item in quick settings (shown only where available) turns it on for the next recording, at 720p with 177-frame bursts. While recording, the camera key or a footer icon fires the burst. Choosing another resolution turns it off with a note, and torch and stabilisation are greyed out. (75da159, b396ecb, 1210c48, 1062d11, 4d29705)
  • Slow-motion videos have continuous sound. The microphone is recorded separately and laid onto the video afterwards, silent over the slow part. Gaps are filled with silence, because the gallery's player used to stall where the burst starts. (d2f30f4, 5ecf21d)
  • Progress and a warning for slow motion. While the phone reads out a burst, a pill counts the frames as they arrive and shows a check mark when all are in. A "Too dark for slow-mo" pill appears when the shot would need an ISO above 1600. (1062d11, 75da159)
  • Recording stops and saves before the phone overheats. Android does not report heat on this phone, so a recording could run until the camera was killed and the file lost. The app now reads the camera sensor, battery and board temperatures itself, shows a warming gauge, and stops with a dialog saying what stopped it and how far to cool. (9b75686, 53aaff0, b34b6df)
  • Pause and Resume keep the picture in video. After resuming, the file had sound but the picture stopped at the first pause, because frames arriving during the pause blocked the camera. Those frames are now discarded, so the picture continues. (bf725f4)
  • The recording time sits in a centred pill. While recording, the time shows in a pill at the centre of the top line (amber or red when the phone is hot), with the remaining recording time beside it once under 20 minutes of storage are left. Paused, a pause mark replaces the blinking dot. (2300928)

items.title: GCam processing and memory
items.text: Merging frames the way GCam does, and making it fit in 4 GB of memory.

items.title: Photo and Night
items.text:
• Night mode on the dial. Night is now a mode of its own. Every shot merges 6 to 12 frames on Auto, planned for low light after the phone measures how much it shakes. A Fast or Accurate switch and a "Hold still" message guide you. (6af567e)
  • Night suggestion in dim light. The phone's light sensor reading shows on the top line when it is dark. After two seconds of dim light, Photo mode offers a button that switches to Night. (6af567e)
  • Merged photos start from the steadiest shot. The app uses the phone's motion sensor to find the steadiest of the first four shots and lines the others up on it. This also works on the front camera and when some shots have no motion data. (414297c, e5740b3, b431298, f8267ed, 3132984)
  • Less colour noise in merged dim-light photos. The merge used to mistake ordinary noise for movement and barely used most frames. It now measures each frame's real noise first. At ISO 5120 it uses 7.2 frames' worth of 12 instead of 1.7, and colour noise is halved. (4debfa1, aef51ae, 72d9dd1)
  • Pink, hazy shadows and magenta tints removed in dim light. Dim shots, worst on the front camera, had pink shadows and a magenta cast. Each photo is now measured and corrected, and dim ones get a gentle shadow lift. HDR and RAW photos are unchanged. (ad7ae19, 0cda30f, c2da80d)
  • Low-light photos are as bright as the preview. The low-light plan aimed one stop darker than the normal preview and now matches it. The brightening of merged dark photos was also too weak (about 1.18 times instead of 1.44) and is now applied correctly. (ea83c42, 7171cf4)
  • Darker bursts when the sky or lights would burn out. When the viewfinder shows bright areas turned pure white, a RAW burst is shot 1 to 3 stops darker. The merge then brings the shadows back up, so those highlights stay recoverable. (5b125a7)
  • Merged bursts keep their natural brightness. A merged burst used to be pulled back down to match the dark viewfinder, undoing the cleaner shadows. Several small mistakes were fixed, so the final photo keeps the brighter, better-exposed result. (7273c43, f9e6c2a, 357f5e6, b616857)
  • HDR shots adapt to the scene. Photo mode's HDR used to take fixed darker and brighter shots. It now picks how much darker or brighter from the bright and near-black areas in the viewfinder, and uses a longer exposure on a steady phone so shadows are less noisy. (6dc3b22)
  • HDR shots fire the moment you press. The app watches how steady the phone is while the viewfinder is open, so it no longer waits half a second. The tap on the shutter no longer counts as shake, so a tripod gets the longer, cleaner exposure. (199c8dd, 8901922)
  • Bracketing is a switch again, on by default. The brighter and darker shots of Photo mode could not be reached any more, because upstream fixed the setting off. Quick settings and Settings now have a Bracketing switch beside Multi-frame. It works on the back camera only (the front camera cannot change exposure between shots, so its extra shots came out the same) and at 12 MP or less (at full size a bracketed stack runs a 4 GB phone out of memory). How it works, and how it differs from Pro's darker burst: Exposure bracketing. (f2512a9, 7c4d773)
  • Photo mode starts at 12 MP with 5 frames and bracketing. A new install, or one that never chose these, gets the 12 MP size cap, Multi-frame on at 5 frames and Bracketing on. Anyone who had picked a size or a frame count keeps it. (ccfd031)
  • A tripod no longer counts as shaky. The motion sensor read a small steady offset, so the low-light plan always chose its shortest exposure. Only real hand tremor is counted now. (caf0538)
  • Multi-frame shots stay inside the camera's allowed ISO range. When the chosen ISO was above what the camera accepts for manual settings, the request was refused. The value is now brought down into range with the same exposure time. (c396169)

items.title: Pro mode and RAW
items.text:
• Pro mode RAW works on the Xperia XZ1 Compact. On the LineageOS build with the RAW add-on by sunplex07, a RAW-only request made the camera crash. The app now also asks for a full-size JPEG with each RAW shot and discards it, which fixes this. (f96b0f3)
  • Corners of RAW photos are no longer dark. The rear camera gave no useful correction for corner darkening, so corners got about 0.23 of the centre's light. A correction measured on this phone is now applied and saved in the RAW file, bringing corners to 0.93 to 0.97. (6f36b8e)
  • RAW photos with noise reduction no longer come out black. Any RAW photo with brightness or colour noise reduction turned on came out solid black. The cause was fixed, which also saves one full-size copy per photo. (11a5c1c)
  • Pro photos keep their deep shadows. Photos developed in the background came out with darker, crushed shadows than the same shot developed directly. Both now handle black the same way, and older RAW files from the app also develop correctly. (33e0f72)
  • Re-render a finished Pro photo as a copy. Develop a Pro photo again with different settings, such as noise reduction, sharpening or exposure, into a new photo next to the untouched original. Start it from the photo's More sheet, or from several selected photos in the gallery. (2feac61, 9742ad3)
  • A built-in noise profile measured on this phone. The profile comes from a tripod test of 20 shots from ISO 40 to 2884. The phone's own profile is up to 3.7 times off, so the measured one is now the default and the system one is labelled as inaccurate here. (f9adbee, 526df14, add4dc5, 0abca2a)
  • The camera's JPEG in Pro mode matches the finished photo. It used to be saved as the full sensor frame and could be turned or flipped differently. It is now cropped to the shot's shape and turned the same way. (8ad6f41)
  • HDR ratio slider in Pro quick settings. A slider from 1 to 20 limits how far the HDR merge may go. The photo info card also shows the limit and the ratio actually used. (0e6b1bd)
  • Pro starts at 8 frames and an HDR ratio of 8. New installs stack 8 RAW frames, and the HDR ratio limit starts at 8 instead of GCam's 9.8. Settings already chosen are kept. (79b0e46)
  • Pro mode says when something is unavailable. ISO and shutter controls are greyed out on cameras without manual exposure, such as the front camera. Tapping a greyed Pro button explains why, and names the RAW add-on by sunplex07 on this phone's back camera. (b3098e3, 6d9e027)

items.title: Memory and keeping the app alive
items.text:
• Pro photos are developed in the background, one at a time. After a single-frame Pro shot, the RAW file is saved at once and developed later by a separate helper that exits after each photo and hands its graphics memory back.
